Network port basics

What is a network port?

A network port is a 16-bit number from 0 to 65535 that identifies a specific service on a host. The IP address finds the machine; the port number finds the process that should receive the traffic.

What is the difference between TCP and UDP ports?

TCP provides ordered, reliable delivery with a connection handshake, while UDP is connectionless and does not confirm delivery. The same port number can be assigned to different services for each protocol, so always check the transport protocol as well as the number.

What are well-known ports?

Well-known ports are the range 0 to 1023, assigned by IANA to core services such as SSH (22), HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443). Registered ports run from 1024 to 49151, and dynamic or private ports from 49152 to 65535.

How do I check whether a port is open?

On Linux, run ss -tlpn for TCP listeners or ss -ulpn for UDP listeners. On Windows, use Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen or Get-NetUDPEndpoint. Every port page on this site includes the exact command for that port and protocol.

How do I block a port?

Use the host firewall: ufw deny PORT/tcp on Ubuntu, an iptables DROP rule on older systems, or New-NetFirewallRule on Windows. Blocking inbound traffic does not stop a local process from listening, so also disable or bind the service to loopback when it is not needed.

How this reference is built and verified

Doudoumy.

An independent reference generated from the IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry, plus clearly marked community conventions. Verify assignments against the official registry before making firewall changes.
